Selling a Utah House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is. Tell us about the property and the timeline.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Utah statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we do not state it.

Utah law sets out when a person occupying land can claim title by adverse possession, and how an owner can remove someone who has no right to be there. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Adverse possession rebuts the presumption of owner possession if property was held and possessed adversely to legal title for at least seven years before the action. (Utah Code 78B-2-208(2); source)
  • Adverse possession may not be established unless the land was occupied and claimed continuously for seven years and the party and predecessors/grantors paid all taxes levied and assessed on the land (property tax payment is required). (Utah Code 78B-2-214; source)
  • Under a written document purporting to convey title (or a court decree/judgment conveying title), property is adversely held if the possessor has occupied it continuously for at least seven years; possession of one lot in a divided tract is not possession of another lot. (Utah Code 78B-2-210; source)
  • An owner or authorized agent may ask law enforcement to immediately remove a trespasser by attesting: unlawful entry, property not open to the public, owner directed the trespasser to leave, not a current/former tenant under a written rental agreement, not an immediate family member, and no pending litigation between them. (Utah Code 78B-6-817(1) (eff. 5/7/2025); source)
  • The owner submits a verified, penalty-of-perjury Complaint to Remove Trespassers with proof of ownership; law enforcement serves a notice to immediately vacate (hand delivery or posting), puts the owner in possession, and may arrest for trespass or other cause. (Utah Code 78B-6-817(2)-(3); source)
  • A wrongfully removed person may sue and recover actual damages, statutory damages equal to triple the fair market rent, court costs and attorney fees. (Utah Code 78B-6-817(5); source)

What we could not confirm

  • Details we could not confirm on an official page are not stated here. Read the statute sections linked above for the full text, and confirm deadlines with the court or county office.

How to sell a Utah house when this applies to you

  1. Write down who is in the house and on what terms: owner, heirs, tenants or occupants with no lease.
  2. Ask the title company what it needs to insure the sale, such as a recorded deed, court papers or a payoff letter.
  3. Get the payoff for any mortgage and the amount of any unpaid property tax. Both are paid from the proceeds at closing.
  4. Compare offers on what you net after repairs, commissions and closing costs. If you want a fast, simple closing, ask for a written cash offer. See we buy houses in Utah.

What a cash sale of a Utah house looks like, step by step

People often ask what actually happens after they contact a cash buyer. Here is the usual order of events for a house in Utah.

  1. Tell us about the property. Use the form on this page or call or text (424) 435-2326. We ask about the address, the condition and what is going on, such as a mortgage, back taxes, tenants or an estate.
  2. Get a written cash offer. We review the details and send a written offer. There is no obligation, and you can turn it down and owe us nothing.
  3. Pick your closing date. You choose the timeline. Some owners need weeks to move out, and others want to close quickly.
  4. The title company handles the paperwork. It checks ownership, pays off any mortgage and any unpaid property tax from the proceeds, and records the deed.
  5. You receive the proceeds. Our offers carry no agent commission, no fees and no closing costs to you.

Documents and information to have ready

You do not need everything below to get an offer, but each item makes the sale smoother and helps the title company work faster.

  • The deed or other proof of who owns the property today.
  • A recent mortgage statement or a payoff figure from the lender.
  • The latest property tax bill, plus any notice of unpaid or delinquent tax.
  • Homeowners association details, including dues and any unpaid assessments, if there is an association.
  • Current leases and the tenants' contact information, if the house is rented.
  • Estate paperwork, such as letters from the court, if you inherited the house.
  • A short list of known repairs. We buy as-is, but honest information avoids surprises.

Listing, selling it yourself or a cash offer: how they compare

Listing with an agent can bring a higher headline price when a house is in good shape and you have time. You pay the commission agreed in your listing contract, and you usually handle repairs, showings and the buyer's inspection requests. Closing depends on the buyer's financing.

Selling it yourself saves the listing commission but puts the marketing, the paperwork and the required Utah disclosures on you. You still need a title company or attorney to close.

Taking a cash offer trades some of the headline price for speed and certainty. We buy as-is, so there are no repairs, no showings and no financing contingency. It tends to fit owners dealing with foreclosure pressure, an inherited house, back taxes, tenants or a move on a deadline. Compare every option on what you net after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not on the headline price.

Questions to ask before you sell in Utah

  • Ask the title company what is owed and what the title company will need at closing.
  • Ask your lender for a written payoff figure good through your expected closing date, and ask whether there is a prepayment penalty.
  • Ask the county assessor whether a pending appeal or exemption affects the bill, and whether any exemption you receive ends when you sell.
  • If the house was inherited, ask the title company which court documents it needs before it will insure the sale.
  • If tenants live in the house, check the lease for its end date and any notice you must give.

These are general questions to start a conversation, not legal advice. Rules in Utah change, so confirm details with the official office or a Utah attorney or tax professional.

More questions about selling in Utah

How fast can I close on a cash sale?

You choose the closing date within what the title company needs to clear ownership and payoffs.

Do I have to clean out or repair the house?

No. We buy houses as-is, so you do not need to make repairs before selling.

Will you buy a house that has tenants in it?

Yes. We buy rentals as-is, occupied or vacant. Tell us about the lease when you request an offer.

What if I owe more on the mortgage than the house is worth?

Tell us the payoff figure. A sale that does not cover the loan may need lender approval, so ask your lender about a short sale before you sign anything.

Can I sell an inherited house before probate is finished?

It depends on who has legal authority to sign. The title company can tell you what court paperwork it needs.

Is there any cost to request an offer?

No. Requesting an offer is free and carries no obligation.

Utah Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my Utah house?

Only by meeting every requirement of the adverse possession statute cited above for the full period. Check the statute and talk to a Utah attorney about your facts.

Can I sell a house that has squatters in it?

Yes. We buy houses as-is, including occupied ones. Tell us who is in the property when you request an offer.

Should I remove a squatter myself?

No. Use the legal process described in the official sources above. Self-help removal can create liability for the owner.

Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Utah statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we do not state it.

Utah statutes set the basic rules between landlords and tenants, including deposits, notices and what happens when a rental is sold. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Landlord must return the deposit balance and prepaid rent, with a written itemization of any deductions, no later than 30 days after the renter vacates and returns possession. (Utah Code 57-17-3(2); source)
  • If the owner fails to comply, tenant may serve a statutory notice; owner then has five business days to comply or owe the full deposit, prepaid rent and a $100 penalty, and possibly court costs and attorney fees if bad faith. (Utah Code 57-17-3(3),(5); source)
  • Owner must give at least 24 hours prior notice of entry into the rental unit, unless the rental agreement provides otherwise. (Utah Code 57-22-4(2); source)
  • Owner may not rent premises unless safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy, and must maintain common areas, electrical, plumbing, heating, hot and cold water, and any air conditioning in operable condition. (Utah Code 57-22-4(1); source)
  • Late fee may not exceed the greater of 10% of rent or $75; a new charge not in the rental agreement is allowed only on a month-to-month tenancy with 15-day notice. (Utah Code 57-22-4(5); source)
  • A tenant on a month-to-month (indefinite, periodic rent) tenancy must be served notice to quit at least 15 calendar days before the end of the month or period. (Utah Code 78B-6-802(1)(b)(i); source)

Utah Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Cash Home Buyers in Utah
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

We buy as-is. Tell us about the property and the timeline.

Utah law requires a landlord to give a specific written notice before filing an eviction, and the number of days depends on the reason. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Nonpayment: tenant is in unlawful detainer if still in possession after a written notice to pay or surrender remains uncomplied with for three business days after service. (Utah Code 78B-6-802(1)(c); source)
  • Lease violation: unlawful assignment/sublet, waste, unlawful business, nuisance or criminal act requires a three calendar days' notice to quit; other covenant violations require a written notice to perform or surrender, uncomplied for three calendar days. (Utah Code 78B-6-802(1)(d)-(h); source)
  • No-cause month-to-month: notice to quit at least 15 calendar days before end of the month or period; tenancy at will: notice of not less than five calendar days. (Utah Code 78B-6-802(1)(b); source)
  • A fixed term ends at expiration without notice; holding over after the specified term is unlawful detainer. (Utah Code 78B-6-802(1)(a); source)
